title: They Don’t Love Lust… They’re Terrified of What They'll Have to Face Without It
paragraphs:
They Don’t Love Lust… They’re Terrified of What They'll Have to Face Without It
The hidden reason so many refuse to let go—and the scandalous grace of Jesus that can rewrite even the darkest heart.
There is a question many Christians quietly ask but few dare say aloud.
"If lust is destroying me... why do I keep protecting it?"
It is one of the most painful contradictions in the human heart.
A man kneels in church on Sunday but falls into pornography on Tuesday night.
A woman loves Jesus deeply, yet secretly feeds fantasies she knows are pulling her away from Him.
Someone deletes sinful images with tears in their eyes...
...only to search for them again hours later.
Why?
If we truly hate sin...
why do we sometimes fight harder to keep it than to kill it?
The answer is far deeper than weak self-control.
It reaches into the wounds of the human soul.
It reaches all the way back to Eden.
And unless we understand it, we may spend years trying to prune branches while never touching the poisoned root.
The Bible never presents lust merely as a physical problem.
It reveals it as a worship problem.

The Greek word often translated "lust" is ἐπιθυμία (epithymia), meaning an intense craving, passionate desire, longing, or over-desire. The word itself is morally neutral in some contexts; Scripture even uses it positively when referring to Christ's desire to eat the Passover with His disciples (Luke 22:15). But when directed toward what God forbids, it becomes a consuming desire that seeks satisfaction apart from Him.
James writes:
Notice something astonishing.
James never says temptation begins with Satan.
He says temptation begins when our own desires drag us away.
Satan may bait the hook.
But our own hearts bite it.
This agrees perfectly with Jeremiah's sobering words:
"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9, ESV)

The Hebrew word translated "deceitful" is עָקֹב ('aqov), carrying the idea of something crooked, insidious, or deceptive. The problem is not merely outward behavior but an inner heart bent away from God by the Fall.
That truth is uncomfortable.
We would rather blame technology.
The culture.
Social media.
Stress.
Our upbringing.
The devil.
But Scripture lovingly exposes the deeper issue because only the real diagnosis leads to the real cure.
Still, why don't people want to let go?
Sometimes it is because lust has quietly become anesthesia.
People who carry rejection often medicate it with fantasy.
People who feel lonely create imaginary intimacy.
People crushed by shame seek temporary escape.
People drowning in anxiety chase momentary pleasure.
Lust promises relief without relationship.
Comfort without commitment.
Pleasure without vulnerability.
Power without sacrifice.
But every promise is counterfeit.
Sin always advertises freedom and delivers chains.
Jesus exposed this plainly:
"Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin." (John 8:34, ESV)
Notice He did not merely say people commit sin.
He said sin enslaves.
Many who refuse to let go are not celebrating their chains.
They have simply worn them so long they mistake them for part of themselves.
This is one of Satan's oldest lies.
"If I lose this sin...
I'll lose myself."
Nothing could be further from the truth.
Because your identity was never meant to be built around your temptations.
It was always meant to be hidden in Christ.
Paul reminds believers:
"Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come." (2 Corinthians 5:17, ESV)
Notice he doesn't say, "You became a slightly improved version."
He says something entirely new has begun.
Another reason people resist surrender is fear.
Not fear of punishment.
Fear of emptiness.
"What if I give this up...
and God doesn't satisfy me?"
That question has echoed since Genesis.
When the serpent approached Eve, he questioned God's goodness before he questioned God's command.
Genesis records:
"Now the serpent was more crafty than any other beast of the field that the LORD God had made..." (Genesis 3:1, ESV)
The Hebrew word עָרוּם ('arum) means crafty, shrewd, or cunning. Satan's strategy was never merely to tempt Eve toward fruit. It was to tempt her into believing God was withholding something better.
That same whisper continues today.
"God doesn't want you happy."
"You're missing out."
"You deserve this."
"It isn't hurting anyone."
"Later you can repent."
Every one of those whispers questions God's character before it attacks His commands.
But Jesus reveals the Father's true heart.
"The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly." (John 10:10, ESV)

The Greek word ζωή (zōē) refers not merely to biological existence but the fullness of life found in fellowship with God. Christ is not trying to steal joy from us. He is rescuing us from counterfeit joy that always expires.
Many people secretly believe they can follow Jesus while negotiating permanent peace with lust.
But Jesus never invited anyone into partial surrender.
He said:
"If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me." (Luke 9:23, ESV)

The Greek word ἀπαρνησάσθω (aparnēsasthō) means to utterly renounce or disown oneself—not to hate one's humanity but to reject the sinful self-rule that places personal desires above Christ. Discipleship is not behavior modification; it is the daily surrender of the throne of the heart.
Yet here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
The answer is not trying harder.
The answer is not white-knuckled determination.
The answer is not endless guilt.
The answer is Jesus.
Many people think Christianity says:
"Stop sinning so Jesus will love you."
The Gospel says something infinitely better:
"Jesus loved you while you were still a sinner."
Paul writes:
This is the scandal of grace.
The Holy One entered the world of the guilty.
The sinless One bore the punishment of sinners.
The Judge stepped down from His bench and took the sentence Himself.
That is why our ministry says:
Not because sin is small.
But because Christ is greater.
The cross never minimizes lust.
It magnifies the mercy that can forgive it, the power that can break it, and the grace that can transform the one enslaved by it.
If lust has become your hiding place, hear this carefully.
Jesus is a better refuge.
If lust has become your comfort, Christ offers a comfort that does not leave guilt in its wake.
If lust has become your identity, Jesus offers you a new name.
If lust has become your prison, Christ still holds the keys.
You are not beyond redemption.
You are not beyond cleansing.
You are not beyond restoration.
The blood of Christ reaches deeper than your darkest secret.
The resurrection is stronger than your strongest addiction.
Perhaps the hardest battle is not deleting a website.
Not uninstalling an app.
Not throwing away hidden images.
The hardest battle is surrendering the belief that sin has something better to offer than Jesus.
That lie dies only when we see Christ for who He truly is: infinitely holy, infinitely gracious, infinitely satisfying.
Psalm 16:11 declares:
"In your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore." (ESV)
Notice that Scripture does not deny pleasure.
It redirects it to its true source.
God is not anti-joy.
He is against everything that destroys real joy.
If this article exposed something you've been hiding, don't disappear in silence.
You may never know how God uses a simple act of obedience to begin someone's journey from bondage to freedom.
Sometimes the reminder you need tomorrow is the one God gave you today.
One surrendered heart can become the testimony that reminds thousands that no chain is stronger than the Savior who breaks it.
